  The City Council is making every effort to follow the spirit and intent of the Brown Act and
 other applicable laws regulating the conduct of public meetings in order to maximize
 transparency and public access.

 In accordance with the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, if you require a disability-
 related modification or accommodation to participate in this meeting, please contact the
 City Clerk’s Office at (661) 267-5151 at least 72 hours prior to the meeting.

 If you require oral Spanish translation, please contact the City Clerk’s Office at (661) 267-

 Your courtesy is requested to help our meetings run smoothly. If you’ll be kind enough to
 follow these simple rules, we can make the best possible use of your time and ours:

  Please refrain from public displays or outbursts, such as unsolicited applause,
  comments, cheering, foul language or obscenities.

   Methods: data collected

• Part 1 and Part 2 crimes handled by the Palmdale Sheriff's Station in 2019
  and 2020 (Los Angeles Sheriff's Department Part I and Part II Data)

• Names, addresses, and types of licensed retail alcohol establishments in
  the City of Palmdale (CA ABC Licenses by City)

• Palmdale city boundaries and US census block groups made up of areas
  that populations ranging from 600 to 2000 people (US Census Data)

• Sociodemographic data for each block group (US Census Data)

 Methods: creating a spatial dataset

• Each crime point geocoded and spatially joined to census block
  groups using ArcGIS Online
• Each licensed retail alcohol establishment within City boundaries
  geocoded and spatially joined to census block groups using ArcGIS
• Densities calculated as:
  • Crime rate - # crimes per 1000 people
  • Alcohol density - # outlets per square mile
• Sociodemographic information added to each census block group.
   Methods: analysis of data

Spatial analysis of the relationships between the density of
licensed retail alcohol establishments and the crime rate in
block groups, taking into account (controlling for)
sociodemographic factors

• GIS Mapping (ArcGIS Online)
• Multilevel Regression Analysis (Stata 17)

   Results: multilevel regression

  Positive associations* were found across both years studied
  (2019 & 2020) between ZIP code 93550 and Part 1 and Part 2
  crime counts.

*Establishing causality is not possible in this case because we used data from past
years and were not able to “control” all conditions in any of the block groups.
Statistically significant associations allow us to make predictions about the number of
crimes associated with an increase in alcohol outlets.
 Results: Palmdale block groups

 • Alcohol outlet density is positively associated with crime rate
  at the block group level
 • A positive association was found across both of the years
  studied (2019 & 2020), for both outlet types (on-premises &
  off-premises).
  • With each additional on-premises establishment (per square mile)
  there is a 23% increase in the likelihood of a PI crime (per 1,000
  pop.)
  • With each additional off-premises establishment (per square mile)
  there is a 67% increase in likelihood of a PI crime (per 1,000 pop.)

Receive and file the monthly and quarterly investment activity reports for June 2022.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council accept the monthly and quarterly investment
activity report for City of Palmdale and Successor Agency for June 2022.

BACKGROUND
Pursuant to Section 16 of the City of Palmdale and Successor Agency Investment
Policy, the City Treasurer shall prepare and present monthly and quarterly reports on
investments to the City Manager/Executive Director and the City Council/Directors.
The reports shall detail the type of investment, name of the issuer, purchase date, date
of maturity, amount of deposit, and rate of interest. This information shall be provided
for all City and Successor Agency pooled investments, as well as for Certificates of
Participation, Revenue Bonds, Tax Allocation Bonds, Assessment Districts and
Community Facilities District accounts which are managed by outside Fiscal Agents.
The monthly and quarterly reports provide a synopsis of the investment activity for the
City of Palmdale and Successor Agency. The reports provide information on assets,
allocations, average maturities, yields, and book valuations.
The interest rates presented are the most current rates available as of the date of this
report.
The market values presented for pooled City and Successor Agency investments are
based on closing prices for the related investment as of the date of this report. This
information was obtained from the Wall Street Journal, Bloomberg Financial Markets,
Capital Market Finances, or other reliable source of market prices.

DISCUSSION
Compliance with Investment Policy

For June, the invested portfolio amount for the City of Palmdale totaled $280,303,953
an increase of $23,472,073 from the previous month, and an increase of $37,075,297
in comparison to last year. The increase in overall portfolio balance from the prior
month is due to new investment purchases made during the month as well as transfers
to the City’s LAIF account.

The par value of Successor Agency’s portfolio as of June was $15,240,849. The
balance increased by $3,745,213 from the last month due to deposits made in to the
Successor Agency LAIF account during the month.

All investments meet criteria appropriate to Section 8 of the Investment Policy. The
portfolios are based on a combination of various investments, including CDs,
Corporate Notes, U.S. Treasury Securities and Government Agency Paper, each
adhering to portfolio percentage limitations.

The Finance Division is the custodian for the City and Successor Agency’s investment
portfolio and follows the three main principles of both entity’s investment policy to 1)
Investment in financial instruments that mitigate the risk of monetary losses stemming
from market fluctuations; 2) Establish and maintain a portfolio that has sufficient
liquidity to allow the City and Successor Agency to meet all anticipated cash
requirements; and 3) Seek out investment instruments that provide a competitive
market rate of return.

Liquidity

One core approach the Finance Division focuses on, is providing liquidity to measure
up to the City and Successor Agency’s operational requirements. Thus, the Finance
Department is currently investing in two pooled funds, LAIF and CAMP. These are
intended for the daily operational activities, used for economic uncertainties and
maintenance needs. The pooled funds provide a higher liquidity ratio to ensure the
City and Successor Agency meet cash flow requirements.

Total LAIF balance for the City of Palmdale at the end of June is $100,077,206, a
$15,000,000 increase compared to the prior month due to deposit made during the
month.

Successor Agency LAIF balance at the end of June was $8,700,688, an increase of
$5,000,000 from the previous month due to deposit made during the month.

CAMP’s balance for City of Palmdale is $249,320 compared to May’s balance of
$249,087, a slight increase due to interest received.

We anticipate the rates to increase in the upcoming months, considering the current
state of the economy. In the current month, CAMP shows better performance than
LAIF in interest rates, however, the historical trend shows that LAIF rates generally
outperform CAMP rates. The difference between the performance of the two funds is
partly due to the varying pool characteristics. CAMP’s portfolio composition is much
more subject to market volatility, resulting in performance variation.

Diversity

The Finance Division aims to diversify the investment portfolios to avoid incurring
unreasonable and avoidable risks regarding specific security types or individual
financial institutions.

City of Palmdale and Successor Agency’s investment portfolios remain strongly
diversified. The monthly reports include all investments held by both entities and
current book values as of June 30, 2022.

ISSUE
Approve First Amendment to Agreement with Eide Bailly, LLP to provide audit services
for an additional amount of $75,000, and a not to exceed amount of $398,792 for a one
(1) year term through June 30, 2023.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:

  1. Approve First Amendment to Agreement A-7499 for audit services between the
  City of Palmdale and Eide Bailly, LLP for a term of One (1) year commencing on
  July 1st, 2022, through June 30th, 2023

  2. Direct the Acting City Attorney to finalize the First Amendment to Agreement A-
  7499 and authorize the Interim City Manager or her designee to execute the
  agreement, including making minor and non-substantive changes.

BACKGROUND
The City of Palmdale is required to have annual audits performed by an independent audit
firm in accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in the United States of
America and the standards applicable to financial audits contained in the Governmental
Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States, the provisions
of the Federal Single Audit Act as amended in 1996, and the U.S. Office of Management
and Budget (OMB) circular A-133 Audits of State and Local Governments and Non-Profit
Organizations.

In 2021 the City engaged in an agreement with Eide Bailly, LLP to provide auditing
services for the City of Palmdale, The Palmdale Civic Authority, the Palmdale Financing
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: First Amendment to Agreement with Eide Bailly
August 3, 2022
Page 2

Authority, the City of Palmdale Housing Authority, and the Palmdale Community
Foundation. In addition to performing financial audits, they have also performed the Single
Audit, an audit of the City’s GANN limit calculation for a two-year term, performing
services for Fiscal Year 2020-21 and Fiscal Year 2021-22.

DISCUSSION
In order to comply with the requirement of new Governmental Accounting Standards
Board (GASB) pronouncements such as GASB Statement No. 87 (Leases), GASB
Statement No. 96 (Subscription Based Information-Technology Arrangements) and
GASB Statement No. 101 (Compensated Absences), the City has determined that
amending the contract to include expanded audit procedures and implementation support
is beneficial to the City. Failure to comply with the GASB Pronouncements can result in
an “unclean” or qualified audit opinion, which may limit a government’s ability to issue
bonds by either prohibiting their issuance or requiring a higher interest rate on those
bonds.
Eide Bailly, LLP is a top 25 CPA and consulting firm. Their knowledge and expertise will
continue to benefit the City, solidifying our financial strength and positioning us for future
growth and stability. Eide Bailly, LLP has extensive experience auditing California Cities,
Counties, School Districts, and Other Special Districts creating a vast knowledge of
California Revised Statutes and California Administrative Codes. The firm also has
extensive experience auditing the City of Palmdale – in depth knowledge of the City’s
Departments and employees including operations, internal controls, and risks making
the potential transition seamless while the new GASB standards are implemented.

FISCAL IMPACT
$75,000; savings due to vacant positions are available in the department’s salary and
benefit accounts. $15,000 is budgeted and available in account 10115001-721410 Cont
Svcs–Audit. $50,000 is to be transferred from 10115001-701000/705000
Salary/Benefits to 10115001-721410 Cont Svcs-Audit to cover this amendment.

for a four (4) year term through March 30, 2026.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:

  1. Approve Second Amendment to professional services Agreement A-7459 with
  Lance, Soll, & Lunghard, LLP for an additional amount of $27,400, not to exceed
  amount of $237,400 for a four (4) year term through March 30, 2026.

BACKGROUND
The City of Palmdale is required to produce annual financial statement package,
commonly known as ACFR (Annual Comprehensive Financial Reports). ACFR is a set of
financial statements for a state, municipality or other governmental entity that comply with
the accounting requirements established by the Governmental Accounting Standard
Board (GASB). It must be audited by an independent auditor using generally accepted
government auditing standards. Because the city’s financial software (Munis) does not
have the capability to produce those statements in a format required by GASB and other
government bodies, third-party software was needed.

On August 1, 2021, the City of Palmdale engaged in an agreement with Lance, Soll, &
Lunghard LLP, a CPA company, to provide CaseWare ACFR implementation, as well as
its training and support. Also included in the agreement was to create a customized
CaseWare templates to assist with the automation of the Annual Comprehensive
 Report to Mayor and City Council

Financial Report (ACFR) that consists of Financial Statements, Cashflow Statement,
Management Discussion and Analyst, Notes, and Statistical Section.

DISCUSSION
The Second amendment to the agreement is being requested to provide additional on-
site professional services to assist in the completion of the City’s Annual Comprehensive
Financial Report (ACFR) for FY 2021-22. The Second amendment will amend the scope
of services to include Senior level assistance to be provided on-site for a 40-hour work
week to assist the Finance Department in completing this project.

Lance, Soll, & Lunghard LLP is the largest accounting firm in Orange County, California
and has been in business for 85 years. Their knowledge and expertise will continue to
benefit the City, solidifying our financial strength and positioning us for future growth and
stability. They have extensive experience in financial reporting, getting the most out of
CaseWare, automating accounting processes and providing support and training to
California Cities, Counties, School Districts, and Other Special Districts.

$27,400; savings due to vacant positions are available in the department’s salary and
benefit accounts. Funds are to be transferred from 10115001-701000/705000
Salary/Benefits to Professional Services 10115001-721960 to cover this amendment.

ISSUE
Adopt Resolution No. CC 2022-085, a resolution of the City Council of the City of
Palmdale, authorizing the submission of the application for the 2022 Local Edward
Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant (JAG) Program.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends the City Council:
  1. Adopt Resolution No. CC 2022-085 authorizing the submission of the application
  for the 2022 JAG grant.
  2. Authorize the City Manager or their designee to execute any documents related
  to the application, acceptance, and implementation of the grant.

BACKGROUND

Since November 2005, the City has contracted for two (2) additional motorcycle
deputies, bringing the total number of motorcycle deputies contracted with the Los
Angeles Sheriff’s Department to five (5) and includes one (1) motorcycle sergeant. The
two additional motor deputies have provided critical services in traffic and crime
deterrence.

Each year the City sets goals to help reduce overall collisions and incidents. The City
proposes to reduce and maintain overall collisions in the City by 4%; reduce speed
related collisions by 4%; reduce DUI/DWI collisions by 5%, and reduce the percentage
of DUI/DWI related collisions involving an injury or fatality by 5% by June 30, 2023. In
2021, DUI/DWI collisions involving injury were reduced by 25.76% and the percentage
of DUI/DWI collisions resulting in a fatality were reduced by 50%. The two grant
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Resolution No. CC 2022-085
Page 2

deputies also issued 2,428 citations for hazardous violations, concentrating on the
speed-related problem areas throughout the City, particularly around school zones. A
total of 269 non-hazardous citations were also issued and 137 traffic related arrests
were made.

The deputies are available to respond to calls for service and will work in coordination
with the City’s Neighborhood Services Department to identify high-risk areas and other
areas of concern, such as school zones. In addition, the deputies are responsible for
conducting DUI/DWI checkpoints and neighborhood traffic operations to reduce speed.

The ten (10) identifiers associated with the grant funded activities include: alcohol
testing, drugs, corrections, crime prevention, DWI, education, evaluation, impaired
driving, policing, and traffic enforcement.

The two (2) motorcycle deputies, partially funded through this grant, will help mitigate
traffic incidents from increasing and provide timely response to citizen complaints. Their
efforts to maintain traffic safety and community safety, law enforcement priorities, will
help reduce the number of overall collisions and incidents.

City staff will submit specific performance measure data as required under the award.
The City’s performance measures correlate to the goals, objectives and deliverables
identified in the grant solicitation.

The City proposes utilizing the 2022 Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Grant (JAG)
program allocation of $50,943 to continue to assist with the cost of two motor deputies.

FISCAL IMPACT
The 2022 JAG grant allocation of $50,943 will be utilized to continue funding two
motorcycle deputies in account 10125002-721836-1072. The general fund will fund the
remaining $404,659 for the cost of the two deputies.

environment.

ISSUE

Approve Memorandum of Understanding Between the City of Palmdale and Antelope
Valley Economic Development and Growth Enterprise (AV EDGE).

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:

  1. Approve Agreement No. A-8013, a Memorandum of Understanding Between the
  City of Palmdale and Antelope Valley Economic Development and Growth
  Enterprise (AV EDGE).

  2. Authorize the City Manager or her designee to prepare and execute all necessary
  documents.

BACKGROUND
AV EDGE was created when the Antelope Valley Board of Trade and the Greater
Antelope Valley Economic Alliance (GAVEA) merged in 2019. Since its inception, the
organization has been a key strategic partner in advancing economic development
initiatives for the Palmdale community and surrounding Antelope Valley region.

The proposed Memorandum of Understanding (“MOU”) would solidify the partnership
between the City and AV EDGE, as well as strengthen the region’s economic
development efforts in response to the pandemic recovery.

The intended purpose of the MOU is to provide a mechanism for AV EDGE to serve as
force multiplier of the City’s existing economic development staff, fostering collaboration
and enhanced services to further regional economic development goals.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Memorandum of Understanding Between the City of Palmdale and AV EDGE
August 3, 2022
Page 2

DISCUSSION
Several Palmdale businesses continue to struggle as a result of COVID-19 related
closures and restrictions. AV EDGE aims to assist Palmdale small businesses, workers
and aid tourism, travel and hospitality businesses that are dealing with the negative
economic impacts created by the pandemic. Through the MOU, AV EDGE would allow
the City to expand the number of services and assistance provided to the small business
community. In addition, AV EDGE will provide quarterly reports detailing the compliance
with a variety of deliverables that focus on business retention, attraction and
expansion efforts. AV EDGE will focus on several deliverables including but not
limited to:
  • Meet with local businesses and industry representatives to understand ongoing
  challenges caused by the pandemic and facilitate resolutions by connecting
  businesses with available resources.
  • Create and update an AV EDGE broker/site selector list to find users for industrial
  and commercial buildings that are vacant because of the negative economic
  impact of the pandemic. A regional site tour with brokers and site selectors will
  take place at least once per calendar year.
  • Business forum to be held at least twice per calendar year.
  • Newsletter and email campaign highlighting new development and regional
  opportunities to be published at least quarterly and on the website.
  • Establish a Business Attraction Task Force that includes members of the City,
  utility companies, and brokers to support regional collaboration and prioritization
  of key projects.
  • Represent the City at a minimum of four (4) industrial or commercial trade shows
  per calendar year.
  • Coordinate tourism and marketing on a regional basis to assist local hotels that
  were impacted by the pandemic to increase occupancy rates. Marketing program
  to be negotiated with the Lancaster and Palmdale Tourism and Business
  Improvement Districts (TBIDs)

FISCAL IMPACT
Up to $650,000.00 of ARPA funds over three years beginning August 1, 2022 through
July 31, 2025.

STRATEGIC PLAN
Goal II: Ensure long-tern fiscal health of the city and maintain funding for services.

  A. Manage resources, costs, and liabilities to ensure the City’s long-term fiscal
  health.

BACKGROUND
The City administers service agreements with contractors that specialize in various
professional disciplines to assist with department operations, such as backflow prevention
device testing, certification, and repair and replacement services.

The Public Works Maintenance Division has approximately 600 backflow prevention
devices that require annual testing and certification. By utilizing a contractor specialized
in these services, it ensures that certifications are completed and submitted to the
regulatory agency on time and comply with required guidelines. The contractor also
 Report to Mayor and City Council

provides test reports and performs visual inspections on each device. This identifies if a
device is not in compliance, is defective, has been vandalized, and/or if there is any other
cause that may affect it passing the certification test. Consequently, City staff is informed
of any needed repairs, replacements, or freeze protection measures. The contractor may
also be used to perform smaller repairs and to rebuild and replace devices which can
include the removal and replacement of an enclosure slab, replacing ball valves, and
excavation to replace elbows, nipples, and unions.

The services provided by the backflow prevention device contractor supplements the
work performed by City Maintenance staff to remain in compliance, meet service
demands, and further the efficiency of operations.

sent electronically to 332 registered vendors in the City’s PlanetBids vendor database.
The solicitation was posted on the City’s website and published in the Antelope Valley
Press on April 26, 2022 and May 1, 2022.

Two (2) responses were received on May 26, 2022 from 1) Greene Backflow (Santa
Clarita, CA) and 2) Verne’s Plumbing, Inc. (Buena Park, CA). However, the latter
company did not meet the bid requirements and as a result the City rejected Verne’s
Plumbing, Inc.’s bid offer in writing on June 1, 2022. Therefore, Greene Backflow’s bid
proposal was the only one evaluated.

exceed $400,000 over the contract term.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:
  1. Award IFB 22-004-3400 As Needed Professional Painting Services to US National
  Corp dba Jimenez Painting Company;
  2. Approve Agreement No. A-7972 with US National Corp dba Jimenez Painting

  7972 with US National Corp dba Jimenez Painting Company in the amount of
  $400,000, including making minimal and/or non-substantive changes.

BACKGROUND
The City administers service agreements with contractors that specialize in various
professional disciplines to assist with department operations, such as painting services.
The professional painting contractor is utilized to perform specialized services on an as
needed basis at various city locations for the Public Works Maintenance Division and the
Public Art program. These as needed professional painting services include, but are not
limited to, the painting and/or primer work on exterior and interior surfaces, wooden or
metal doors, fascia, rafter tails, wrought iron fencing, City standard light poles, backflow

or irrigation controller enclosures, window casing and security screening, and public art
pieces and surfaces.

The services provided by the painting contractor are used in conjunction with work
performed by City staff to meet increasing service demands, address deferred
maintenance, and further the efficiency of operations to maintain safe and attractive
facilities, public spaces, and infrastructure for the community.

DISCUSSION
The City released Invitation for Bids No. 22-004-3400 for As Needed Professional
Painting Services on April 26, 2022. Notification of the IFB release was sent electronically
to 52 registered vendors in the City’s PlanetBids vendor database. The solicitation was
posted on the City’s website and published in the Antelope Valley Press on April 26, 2022
and May 1, 2022.

Five (5) responses were received on May 26, 2022. Three staff evaluators determined
that US National Corp dba Jimenez Painting Company (Pacoima, CA) was the best
responsive proposal based on the following evaluation criteria:

ISSUE
Notice of Completion - Accept completed project with Nu Line Technologies, LLC., for
PN 751-B, Sanitary Sewer Pipeline Trenchless Rehabilitation Project, at various
locations throughout the City.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:
  1. Accept completed project with Nu Line Technologies, LLC., for PN 751-B,
  Sanitary Sewer Pipeline Trenchless Rehabilitation Project, at various locations
  throughout the City, and
  2. Authorize the Interim City Manager or her designee to execute and file a Notice
  of Completion.

BACKGROUND
Project No. 751-B, Sanitary Sewer Pipeline Trenches Rehabilitation Project, carried out
the trenchless rehabilitation of sixteen (16) pipeline sections of various lengths within
the City’s existing sewer system using cured-in-place pipe (CIPP and UV-CIPP)
trenchless methods only. Work was also included traffic control, traffic control plan
development, and material certification submittals. All work was performed within the
existing right of way.

DISCUSSION
All construction work for this project has been completed. To release funds being held
as retention (five percent of each progress payment), it is necessary for the City Council
to accept the project and for a Notice of Completion to be filed.

FISCAL IMPACT
This project was funded through Sewer Maintenance Assessment District Funds (254),
which have been allocated in Account No. U0003. The original construction contract
amount for this project was $172,300.00 and the final construction cost was
$163,128.93, which represents a 5.3% decrease. This decrease is due to field
conditions that prevented lining of one section in the system. Thirty-five (35) days after

DISCUSSION
During the pandemic the cost of construction of affordable housing increased, the
materials including lumber, drywall, insulation and concrete. The California Department
of General Services Construction Cost Index increased 10.01% from 2020 to 2021, from
7,041 to 7,746, and 15.22% from 2021 to 2022, from 7,746 to 8,925.
The Housing Authority of the City of Palmdale assists Developers with gap financing to

SUBJECT:  ADOPT RESOLUTION NO. CC 2022-087, A RESOLUTION OF
  THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF PALMDALE MAKING
  LEGALLY REQUIRED FINDINGS AND EXTENDING REMOTE
  TELECONFERENCE PARTICIPATION FOR MEETINGS OF
  THE CITY COUNCIL AND/OR ITS RELATED OR
  SUBORDINATE LEGISLATIVE BODIES

ISSUE
Adopt Resolution No. CC 2022-087, a Resolution of the City Council of the City of
Palmdale authorizing remote teleconference participation for meetings of the City
Council and/or its subordinate legislative bodies for an additional 30-day period.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:
  1. Approve the resolution to thereby extend, for an additional 30-day period, the
  authority of the City Council, and all related and/or subordinate legislative bodies,
  to participate remotely in properly noticed meetings.

BACKGROUND
Since October 1, 2021 and through January 1, 2024, AB 361 has temporarily amended
the Ralph M. Brown Act (California Government Code § 54950 et seq.) to provide more
flexibility regarding participation in public meetings from a remote location. In layman’s
terms AB 361 allows “zoom” meetings if specified requirements are met.
If the City Council authorizes remote meetings, such authorization must expire no later
than 30 days from the initial authorization. The City Council is authorized to thereafter
extend the authorization if it makes one of various specified findings.
AB 361 requires several procedural safeguards to protect public participation during a
remote meeting, key ones of which are summarized as follows:
  1. The public must have the ability to address the legislative body directly and must
  be given information on how to address the legislative body;
  2. The public must be provided with either a call-in or internet-based service option;
  3. The legislative body must stop the meeting if the call-in or internet-based option
  fails;

  4. The legislative body cannot require that public comments be submitted in
  advance (although this option can be provided);
  5. Public speakers cannot be required to pre-register for public comment (except as
  required by an independent call-in or internet platform);
  6. Members of the public must be given a reasonable time to register to provide
  public comment; and
  7. Agencies that provide a timed public comment period shall not close the public
  comment period until that time period has expired.
DISCUSSION
The City Council adopted an initial AB 361 Resolution on June 15, 2022. A subsequent
resolution adopted on July 13, 2022 is set to expire on August 13, 2022. An extension
of authority to remotely participate is allowed if (1) the state of emergency continues,
and (2) a resolution with required findings has been adopted within the last 30 days.
The proposed resolution would be immediately effective and allow members of
legislative bodies to continue to participate remotely for an additional thirty days if the
agenda for the meeting has included the legally required participation noticing. The
resolution would also allow the City Manager (or designee) to opt to not include such
noticing, as there may be instances where it would be impractical, due to staffing
considerations, to allow remote participation in meetings.
FISCAL IMPACT
There is no fiscal impact associated with this action.

  WHEREAS, Government Code § 54953(e) expressly allows cities to, during the
existence of a state of emergency declared by the Governor pursuant to Government
Code § 8625, allow teleconference participation in city meetings;

  WHEREAS, on March 4, 2020, the Governor declared a state of emergency and
such declaration continues to be in effect;

  WHEREAS, state and local officials have imposed or recommended measures to
promote social distancing, including requirements to not return to work within specified
time frames for people who have tested positive for COVID-19;

  WHEREAS, the City Council adopted Resolution No 2022-081 within the last thirty
days, authorizing exemption from the requirements of Government Code section
54953(b)(3) from July 13, 2022 until August 13, 2022.

NOW THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF
PALMDALE DOES HEREBY FIND, DETERMINE, RESOLVE AND ORDER AS
FOLLOWS:

  SECTION 1. The Recitals set forth above are correct and are incorporated by
reference.

  SECTION 2. The City Council finds that the state of emergency declared by the
Governor remains in effect and state officials continue to impose or recommend
measures to promote social distancing. Therefore, for agendas which include all the
noticing required by Government Code § 54953(e), the City Council and its related
and/or subordinate bodies, by this Resolution, shall continue to be exempt from the
requirements of Government Code section 54953(b)(3) until the end of the day on

SUBJECT:  ACCEPT GRANT FROM THE CITY OF PALMDALE TO THE

  AFFORDABLE HOUSING

ISSUE
Accept Grant from the City of Palmdale to the Housing Authority of the City of Palmdale
of $1,200,000 of United States Department of the Treasury of Coronavirus Local Fiscal
Recovery Funds (CSLRF Funds) under the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) for
development of affordable housing in the City of Palmdale.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the Housing Authority:
  1. Accept Grant from the City of Palmdale to the Housing Authority of the City of
  Palmdale of $1,200,000 of United States Treasury of Coronavirus Local Fiscal
  Recovery Funds (CSLRF Funds) under the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA)
  for development of affordable housing in the City of Palmdale; and
  2. Authorize the City Manager or their designee to execute documents and take all
  necessary actions to implement the approved actions.

BACKGROUND
The City of Palmdale was awarded $35,445,019 by the United States Treasury of
Coronavirus Local Fiscal Recovery Funds (CSLRF Funds) under the American Rescue
Plan Act (ARPA). Among the eligible uses of ARPA funds is the investment in affordable
housing to increase the supply for low-income residents and the mitigation of financial
hardship experienced by certain types of entities due to the negative economic impacts
resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic.
 Report to Chair and Commissioners of the Housing Authority
Re: Grant from City of ARPA funds
August 3, 2022
Page 2

DISCUSSION
During the pandemic the cost of construction of affordable housing increased, the
materials including lumber, drywall, insulation and concrete. The California Department
of General Services Construction Cost Index increased 10.01% from 2020 to 2021, from
7,041 to 7,746, and 15.22% from 2021 to 2022, from 7,746 to 8,925.
The Housing Authority of the City of Palmdale assists Developers with gap financing to
develop and rehabilitate units that are affordable to eligible households that are Extremely
Low, Very Low and Low Income.
The Housing Authority proposes to loan or grant the ARPA funds granted by the City and
program income received through repayment of the funds for the development of eligible
affordable housing projects.

FISCAL IMPACT
Funds are available in account 15818503-737100-1332 ARPA Affordable Housing.

Goal III: Invest in infrastructure to improve community livability and to plan and maintain
  safe and attractive neighborhoods, streets and facilities.
  C.  Plan and maintain safe and attractive neighborhoods, streets, facilities, and
  public spaces with exciting programming that promotes active fun for everyone.

   City Council Staff Report
DATE:  AUGUST 3, 2022
TO:  HONORABLE MAYOR AND CITY COUNCIL
FROM:  CITY MANAGER’S OFFICE – FINANCE DIVISION
DISTRICT:  ALL
SUBJECT:  ADOPT RESOLUTION NO. CC 2022-065 A RESOLUTION OF THE
  CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF PALMDALE RESTATING IN ITS
  ENTIRETY THE PALMDALE MASTER SCHEDULE OF FEES AND
  REPEALING RESOLUTION NO. CC 2021-057

ISSUE
Adopt Resolution No. CC 2022-065 a Resolution of the City Council of the City of
Palmdale restating in its entirety the Palmdale Master Schedule of Fees and Repealing
Resolution No. CC 2021-057.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:

  1. Adopt Resolution No. CC 2022-065 to authorize the proposed fees and charges
  for the fees, charges, and requirements set forth in the City of Palmdale Master
  Schedule of Fees for Service, effective July 1, 2022, and attached hereto;

  2. Repeal Resolution No. CC 2021-057;

BACKGROUND
Periodically, the City Council adopts Fee Resolutions, which 1) revise existing fees,
rates, or charges; 2) establishes new fees, rates, or charges; or 3) revise headings or
descriptive language for existing fees for the City's operating departments.

On June 15, 2021, the City Council adopted Resolution No. CC 2021-057 adopting a
citywide fee schedule that was to be implemented in a biennial phased in approach, with
some increases taking effect July 1, 2021 and some taking effect July 1, 2022.
Resolution No. CC 2021-057 authorized proposed rates for Planning, Engineering and
Building & Safety, in a biennial phase approach.

Additionally, the 2021-22 fee schedule was reformatted and as part of that process some
information from the previously adopted 2017 Fee Schedule was unintentionally omitted.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Adopt Resolution No. CC 2022-065 Restating in its Entirety the Palmdale Fee
Schedule and Repealing Resolution No. CC 2021-057
August 3, 2022
Page 2

Upon thorough review, the proposed Master Schedule of Fees has corrected this matter,
restoring missing fees and policies.

DISCUSSION
The State Constitution provides the authority for cities to impose user fees and
regulatory fees for services and activities, however the fees may not exceed the
estimated reasonable cost of providing the service or performing the activity.

In order to better achieve the City’s policy regarding cost recovery goals and to minimize
General Fund subsidies for services provided staff has identified inefficiencies, missing
fees and/or processes.

Staff recommends that the City Council adopts Resolution No. CC 2022-065 to authorize
proposed adjustments to the Palmdale Master Schedule of Fees for certain departments
detailed in this staff report and presented in the attached Master Schedule of Fees,
effective July 1, 2022.

PARKS AND RECREATION

DryTown has two new rental items, glow in the dark inner tubes for evening events and
smaller sized shade cabanas. Both of these items have been added to the fee schedule.
With the CPI increase last year, cabana pricing for the larger units were changed to an
odd figure. For marketing purposes, this fee is proposed to be slightly reduced. Similarly,
for marketing and efficiency all fees have been increased to the nearest .25, which has
historically been the practice. Fees and policies from the 2017 Fee Schedule which
were unintentionally omitted in subsequent schedule updates have been restored.

One omitted policy, which defines how recreation program fees are to be established
has been updated to reflect current recommendations, trends and practices. A
recommendation from the user fee study conducted by Revenue & Cost Specialists,
LLC suggested that the City Council develop a conscious policy as to what programs
should be subsidized with tax monies in promoting social benefit and to what extent.
Likewise, current industry best practices have shifted to a subsidy and cost recovery
policy, titled pyramid methodology by BerryDunn.com and GreenPlay LLC. This
methodology originated in the 1990’s and is now widely practiced across the United
States. The resulting pyramid model illustrates appropriate program subsidy levels and
cost recovery targets, which provides the framework necessary for decision making.
The bottom of the pyramid consists of basic services free to the public in the interest of
social and community benefit. The top of the pyramid consists of services that are
structured, specialized or are used by special interest groups or individuals. Services at
the bottom of the pyramid are subsidized by City revenues, conversely services at the
top of the pyramid are incrementally off-set by participation fees. Reference Fee
Schedule attachment, Parks & Recreation Cost Recovery Pyramid.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Adopt Resolution No. CC 2022-065 Restating in its Entirety the Palmdale Fee
Schedule and Repealing Resolution No. CC 2021-057
August 3, 2022
Page 3

Following the cost recovery methodology noted above, all associated parks and
recreation program, league, admission, merchandise and processing fees have been
itemized and added to the fee schedule. Most all proposed fees remain the same with
two exceptions. New fees are called out in the fee description, these are expanded
programs or admission offerings to better serve residents. In addition, DryTown Water
Park fees are proposed to increase, 20% or less. Due to increased demand, a new
season pass alternative has also been incorporated. Our practice has been to increase
water park fees bi-annually, due to COVID we have not increased park fees since 2018.

GIS FEES
The City has historically charged a 5% GIS fee on various Building & Safety, Planning
and Engineering fees to recoup the City’s GIS cost, which include software and labor
required to track and maintain locations of any and all permits, assets and any additional
items that have a geographical location within the City. Extensive staff time is required
to maintain accurate GIS information, which is then used by City staff and the public for
purposes of permitting, plan check, inspections, engineering and various aspects of
planning. The public is also provided limited access to the City’s GIS data, which aids in
the application processes. See Exhibit J, attached.

ECONOMIC & COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT
Building & Safety and Planning divisions are proposing to add an Expedited Fee for the
below services. The inclusion of this fee in the City’s Master Schedule of Fees is a
response to the developer community and the desire to have the option to request and
pay for an expedited turnaround time on services. This is an optional fee.

Exhibit A – Building & Safety
   Expedited Plan Check

Exhibit O - Planning
   Expedited Conditional Use Permit (CUP)
   Expedited Preliminary Project Review to Development Advisory Board (DAB)
   Expedited Site Plan Review

NEIGHBORHOOD SERVICES
There are no proposed changes to fees in the Neighborhood Services section of the
Master Schedule of Fees, however, additional language has been added to show the
specific code violations that are subject to administrative citations, as well as the City’s
policies for handling repeat violations, late payments and collections. See Exhibit K,
attached.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Adopt Resolution No. CC 2022-065 Restating in its Entirety the Palmdale Fee
Schedule and Repealing Resolution No. CC 2021-057
August 3, 2022
Page 4

CONCLUSION
Any action by the City to levy a new fee or service charge or to approve an increase in
an existing fee or service must be approved by ordinance or resolution. Before any new
fee or service charge can be added to the Palmdale Fee Resolution, a public hearing
must be held, and reasonable notice must be provided to the members of the
community.

As such, Staff recommends that the City Council Adopt Resolution No. CC 2022-065
and Repeal Resolution No. CC 2021-057, authorizing the proposed fees and charges
for the fees, charges, and requirements set forth in the City of Palmdale Master
Schedule of Fees for Service, effective July 1, 2022.

PUBLIC NOTICE PROCESS
A Public Hearing Notice regarding the citywide fee resolution was published in the local
newspaper of general circulation on June 1, 2022, June 8, 2022, June 14, 2022, June
19, 2022, June 26, 2022, July 24, 2022 and again on August 2, 2022 at which time the
public was invited to make oral and written presentation as part of the regularly
scheduled meeting prior to the adoption of Resolution No. CC 2022-065. Additionally,
written notice has been provided to interested parties at least 14 days prior to the public
meeting to any interested party who filed written requests for mailed notice of meeting
on new or increased development related fees or service charges.

FISCAL IMPACT
Resolution No. CC 2022-065, if adopted, would allow certain fees to be adjusted and
policies to be enacted, which will allow the City to better recoup costs and continue
providing services to the community.

Definitions:
1. Agencies with proof of Internal Revenue Code IRC 501 (c) (3) (4) (5) and (6) are considered non-profits.
2. Commercial use is defined as an event held for the purpose of generating monetary gain for the event sponsor(s).
3. Direct program costs are exclusively incurred as a result of the program and are frequently variable, adjusting as program participation
  varies. Direct cost examples include part-time personnel, supplies, contract services and equipment. DryTown direct costs include the
  preceding expenses in addition to: full-time salaries, park utilities and equipment.
4. Indirect program costs that are shared among several programs and are necessary to execute general day-to-day operations. Indirect
  cost examples include personnel overhead, utilities and custodial expenses. Indirect costs are not considered as fees and charges
  are determined.
Policies
1. Non-profit with verifiable status of IRC 501 (c) (3) (4) (5) or (6) are eligible for a 25% facility reservation rate reduction. Unless otherwise
  specified, facility reservation fees that are eligible for a rate reduction are noted by an *. Rate reductions do not apply to personnel fees,
  facility deposits or equipment rental. Similarly, program fees for non-residents will increase 25% and DryTown admission fees for
  non-residents will increase 15%. Services subject to non-resident increase are noted by an **.
2. Unless otherwise specified, the rate for use of facilities for commercial purposes shall be charged at 200% of the hourly reservation fee,
  in addition to 5% gross admission ticket sales and gross alcohol sales. These fees may be reduced or waived if the applicant can
  demonstrate that residents of the City of Palmdale benefit from the use of facilities or the services being provided.
3. Unless otherwise specified, set-up and clean-up charges are comprised of applicable facility hourly reservation rates.
4. Park parking lots are generally not available for exclusive use reservations. If exclusivity can be accommodated and if parking fees are
  charged by the renter, 25% of parking fees collected are to be paid to the City.
5. Parks & Recreation program and service fees are established by following specified cost recovery policies. Fees and charges are
  determined by identifying direct costs if providing services and apply the cost recovery goals stated below. Direct program costs are
  referenced in the definitions section. It is widely accepted that park and recreation systems are publicly financed, and therefore offer free
  or affordable services. The level of program subsidy will be based on an assessment of the community or social benefit, local market and
  economic conditions. As services have a greater appeal to individuals or groups of individuals, it is appropriate to charge fees for the
  services at an increasing rate of cost recovery. Cost recovery target categories include: Community Benefit/Access, free; Community
  Benefit, 0-25%; Balanced Beneficiaries, 25-50%; Substantial Individual Benefit, 50-75%; Exclusive Individual Benefit, 75-100%.
  Cost recovery categories are further defined in Exhibit L-1.
General Fees
1. Unless otherwise specified, a special event application processing fee of $250 may be charged for staff services required to process the
  application, which may include coordination with other City departments, or State and County government agencies. The fee is
  non-refundable and does not guarantee approval of the application.
2. Unless otherwise specified, fees for personnel shall be calculated at hourly rate for staff wages, plus 45% for full-time benefits or 15%
  for part-time benefits and a 25% administrative fee. Unless the use warrants otherwise, staff will be scheduled to be on-site
  one-half hour before and after use.

ISSUE
Adopt Resolution No. CC 2022-084, a Resolution of the City Council of the City of
Palmdale approving a plan of finance for the issuance of the California Municipal
Finance Authority revenue bonds (Waste Management Project) in an aggregate amount
not to exceed $355,000,000 as part of a plan to finance certain qualified solid waste
disposal facility projects. A portion of the principal amount of the Bonds, in an amount
not to exceed $25,000,000, will be used to finance the following projects (collectively,
the “Project”) located within the City of Palmdale (the “City”) at Palmdale Landfill, 1200
W. City Ranch Road, Palmdale, California, 93551.

RECOMMENDATION
Adopt Resolution No. CC 2022-084, a Resolution of the City Council of the City of
Palmdale approving a plan of finance for the issuance of the California Municipal
Finance Authority revenue bonds (Waste Management Project) in an aggregate amount
not to exceed $355,000,000 as part of a plan to finance certain qualified solid waste
disposal facility projects. A portion of the principal amount of the Bonds, in an amount
not to exceed $25,000,000, will be used to finance the Project located within the City at
Palmdale Landfill, 1200 W. City Ranch Road, Palmdale, California, 93551.

BACKGROUND
USA Waste of California, Inc., a corporation duly organized and existing under the laws
of the State of Delaware, Antelope Valley Recycling and Disposal Facility, Inc., a
corporation duly organized and existing under the laws of the State of California, Waste
Management, Inc., a corporation duly organized and existing under the laws of the State

of Delaware, and/or affiliates thereof (collectively, the “Borrower”), have requested that
the California Municipal Finance Authority (the “Authority”) issue exempt facility revenue
bonds in one or more series from time to time in an aggregate principal amount not to
exceed $355,000,000 (the “Bonds”) as part of a plan of finance to finance certain qualified
solid waste disposal facility projects pursuant to section 142(a)(6) of the Internal Revenue
Code of 1986 (the “Code”).

A portion of the principal amount of the Bonds, in an amount not to exceed $25,000,000,
will be used to finance the following projects located within the City of Palmdale at
Palmdale Landfill, 1200 W. City Ranch Road, Palmdale, California, 93551: (a)
improvements to existing landfill facilities, including but not limited to (i) construction of
new disposal cells and liners within currently permitted acreage, (ii) additions and
improvements to the leachate collection and treatment system, including leachate
trenching, (iii) additions and improvements to the methane gas systems, including
collection, processing and treatment systems for the capture, conversion and/or
distribution of landfill gas, (iv) installation of new liners for intermittent and final closure of
completed sections of the landfill facilities, (v) site and/or land improvements, and
construction of building facilities, (vi) acquisition of equipment to be used at the landfill
facilities, and (vii) acquisition of equipment, land and other assets necessary to support
the foregoing additions and improvements and to place them into service; and (b)
improvements to existing collection (hauling) and transfer station facilities, including but
not limited to (i) acquisition of solid waste disposal and recycling trucks and support
vehicles, (ii) acquisition of solid waste disposal and recycling containers and related
equipment, (iii) acquisition of solid waste sorting and processing and recycling equipment,
(iv) site and/or land improvements, (v) the construction of one or more buildings for
supporting operations of the Project and (vi) acquisition of other equipment and assets
necessary to support the foregoing improvements and place them into service.

DISCUSSION
The CMFA is a political subdivision of the state of California established under the Joint
Exercise of Powers Act for the purpose of issuing tax-exempt and taxable conduit bonds
for public and private entities throughout California. The CMFA is authorized to issue
bonds to promote economic development and public benefit. It has issued over $25
billion of bonds for more than 330 jurisdictions within the State of California. To initiate
such financing and for the Borrower to obtain financing, the City must conduct a public
hearing and approve the CMFA's issuance of indebtedness.

 Approval by the government jurisdiction in which the proposed facilities are located is a
requirement of Section 147(f) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 (IRS Code).

The Bonds to be issued by the CMFA for the Project will be the sole responsibility of the
Borrower, and the City will have no financial, legal, moral obligation, liability or
responsibility for the Project or the repayment of the Bonds for the financing of the
Project. All financing documents with respect to the issuance of the Bonds will contain

SUBJECT:  INTRODUCE AND ADOPT ORDINANCE NO. 1592, AMENDING

  OF CHAPTER 5.04 (BUSINESS REGULATION) OF TITLE 5
  (BUSINESS LICENSES, TAXES, AND REGULATION) OF THE
  PALMDALE MUNICIPAL CODE TO BAN FLAVORED TOBACCO

ISSUE
Introduce and Adopt Ordinance No. 1592, amending section 5.04.670
(Tobacco/Smoking Product Retailer) of Chapter 5.04 (Business Regulation) of Title 5
(Business Licenses, Taxes and Regulation) of the Palmdale Municipal Code banning
Flavored Tobacco Products.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council conduct a public hearing and then introduce and
adopt ordinance No. 1592.

BACKGROUND
Tobacco use is one of the leading causes of preventable death in the United States.
Electronic cigarettes use flavored nicotine that is sold and consumed in thousands of
flavors that appeal to youth, such as bubblegum and cotton candy. These flavors hide
the harshness of nicotine, making initiation of nicotine use more appealing to youth. It is
the purpose and intent of the City to provide for the public health, safety and welfare of
the community, particularly youth, by prohibiting the sale or distribution of flavored
tobacco products.

On December 3, 2019, the City Council adopted Ordinance No. 1535, prohibiting the
sale of flavored electronic cigarette and tobacco products in the City of Palmdale.
However, to accommodate the sale of a tobacco retailer’s existing stock of flavored
electronic cigarette and tobacco products, to adjust inventories and accommodate the
tobacco retailer’s substitution of alternative products for sale, the City Council delayed
implementation of this ordinance. Due to the impact of Covid-19 this delay was
extended on July 14, 2020 with Ordinance No. 1548 and again on March 2, 2021 with
Ordinance No. 1560.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Proposed Ordinance No. 1592
August 3, 2022
Page 2

In August 2020, Senate Bill 793 passed which prohibited the sale of flavored tobacco in
the State of California. In addition, a referendum, the California Flavored Tobacco
Products Ban, qualified for the ballot as a veto referendum which suspended SB 793
until after the November 8, 2022 statewide general election.

On February 16, 2022, the City Council conducted a Public Hearing for proposed
ordinance No. 1580 continuing a temporary suspension of PMC Section 5.04.670(H)(4)
of the Palmdale Municipal Code, prohibiting the sale of flavored electronic cigarette
products, until February 1, 2023. The City Council did not conduct a vote for proposed
Ordinance No. 1580, thus ending the extensions and implementing the original
ordinance No. 1535, prohibiting the sale of flavored electronic cigarette and tobacco
products.

DISCUSSION
Proposed Ordinance No. 1592 amends Title 5 (Business Licenses, Taxes and
Regulation) Chapter 5.04 (Business Regulation) Section 5.04.670 (Tobacco/Smoking
Product Retailer) of the Palmdale Municipal Code regarding the sale and distribution of
Flavored Tobacco Products. “Flavored tobacco product” shall mean tobacco/smoking
products containing, as a constituent or additive, an artificial or natural flavor of an herb
or spice which emit a taste or smell, other than the taste or smell of tobacco, including
but not limited to mint, menthol, spearmint, wintergreen, strawberry, grape, orange,
clove, cinnamon, pineapple, vanilla, coconut, licorice, cocoa, chocolate, cherry, candy,
dessert, alcoholic beverages, or coffee, that is a characterizing flavor of the product, or
the smoke or vapor produced by the product. Flavored tobacco product does not
include premium cigars, shisha, loose leaf tobacco, or products approved by the Food
and Drug Administration for sale as a tobacco cessation product or other therapeutic
purposes, where the product is marketed and sold solely for such an approved purpose.
This Ordinance is exempt from the requirements of the California Environmental Quality
Act (“CEQA”) pursuant to State CEQA Guidelines because there is no possibility that
this Ordinance or its implementation would have a significant negative effect on the
environment. (14 Cal. Code Regs.§ 15061(b)(3)).

If approved, the ordinance shall commence on January 1, 2023, making the sale or
distribution of flavored tobacco products prohibited, and no permit shall be issued under
this section to any such activity. This ordinance shall become effective on August 12,
2022. The changes to the municipal code caused by this ordinance shall take effect on
January 2, 2023, unless the referendum against SB 793 should fail, in which case this
ordinance shall not have any effect, and the municipal code shall remain unchanged.

FISCAL IMPACT
Minimal loss of sales tax revenue generated from sales of Flavored Tobacco Products.

ISSUE
Hold a Public Hearing and adopt Ordinance No. 1593, an Ordinance of the City Council
of the City of Palmdale adding Chapter 9 (Unlawful Possession of a Catalytic Converter
Prohibited) of Title 10 (Vehicles and Traffic) of the Palmdale Municipal Code establishing
regulations prohibiting the unlawful possession of catalytic converters in the City.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:
  1. Continue the Public Hearing and adoption of Ordinance No. 1593 to August 17,
  2022.

BACKGROUND
Catalytic converters are an external component of a vehicle, accessible from the
underside of a parked car. They convert most of a vehicle’s emissions into less harmful
forms, improving air quality and vehicle performance. As part of their construction,
catalytic converters contain valuable materials such as platinum, palladium, and
rhodium, rare metals that command ever-increasing prices on the recyclables market.

Catalytic converter thefts are on the rise because individuals are incentivized to commit
catalytic converter thefts for multiple reasons including, but not limited to 1). The ease
and undetectable nature of committing such thefts, potentially in a matter of seconds
and using common tools such as a reciprocating saw; 2). The ability to recycle catalytic
converters at scrap mental yards for high dollar amounts ranging from $200 to $1,200

prohibiting the unlawful possession of catalytic converters in the City

per catalytic converter; and 3). Loopholes in legislation protecting criminals from
prosecution unless a victim can be identified.
A report by the National Insurance Crime Bureau stated that the increase in catalytic
converter thefts has been dramatic. In 2018, there were 1,298 catalytic converter thefts
for which a claim was filed. In 2019, it was 3,389 thefts with a claim. In 2020, catalytic
converter thefts jumped to an astounding 14,433, a 325% increase in a single year.
Though this reporting does not account for all catalytic converter thefts, it does examine
the trend of catalytic converter thefts.

DISCUSSION
The City of Palmdale is no exception to this national trend with residents and the City
being victimized by this practice. To date, the Los Angeles County Sheriff Department
Palmdale Station reported 184 catalytic converter theft. There is currently no City, State,
or Federal legislation applicable within the City of Palmdale to define and punish catalytic
converter thefts absent an identifiable victim. Additionally, there is currently no City, State,
or Federal legislation applicable within the City of Palmdale requiring individuals to
provide proof to law enforcement as to how they obtained catalytic converters. This limits
law enforcement’s ability to protect the public by preventing catalytic converter thefts and
seizing suspected stolen catalytic converters when there is no identifiable victim present.
Preventing and punishing these crimes at present is nearly impossible due to the ease
and speed with which catalytic converters thefts are committed and the difficulty of tracing
a particular catalytic converter back to its prior owner (the victim), because catalytic
converters typically have no identifying markers.
Individuals in possession of stolen catalytic converters can recycle them for a substantial
profit at a relatively low risk, while victims are forced to pay for costly repairs. By
criminalizing the mere possession of an unattached catalytic converter absent proof of
ownership or lawful possession, the attached ordinance would combat this criminal
activity by (1) Achieving deterrence by establishing zero-tolerance for catalytic converter
thefts; (2) Establishing sanctions for possessing stolen catalytic converters; (3)
Preventing criminals from profiting from the sale and recycling of stolen catalytic
converters; (4) Providing indirect justice to the victims of catalytic converter theft cases
that have gone or will go unsolved for the reasons discussed above; and (5) Minimizing
the fiscal and personnel impact on the City of Palmdale and the Los Angeles County
Sheriff’s Department by reducing time invested in deterring and investigating catalytic
converter thefts.
FISCAL IMPACT
There is no fiscal impact associated with introducing Ordinance No. 1593

ISSUE
Adopt Resolution No. CC 2022-089, a Resolution of the City Council of the City of
Palmdale Directing City Staff and the Sheriff to not Enforce Against the Public COVID-
Related Mask Orders of the Los Angeles County Department of Health.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council adopt Resolution No. CC 2022-089.

BACKGROUND

On July 21, 2022, the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health (Health
Department) announced that for the second week in a row the number of COVID cases
and the number of COVID related hospitalizations have pushed the county into the “high”
level. Had the hospitalization not decreased by Thursday July 28, 2022, a new mask order
would have gone into effect on Friday July 29, 2022.

DISCUSSION

The Los Angeles County Health Department is the public health agency for the City of
Palmdale. The Health Department can enforce health orders, generally through warnings
and citations that are issued through visits to businesses. The Health Department recently
reported that less than 1 percent of the businesses in the county have received citations.

The Center for Disease Control (CDC) has established the concept of “community level”
which uses various criteria to help counties determine the prevention steps to be taken
based on the COVID-19 levels in an area. The three different community levels are low,
medium and high.

On July 21, 2022, the Health Department announced that for the second week in a row the
number of COVID cases and the number of COVID related hospitalizations have pushed
the county into the “high” level. The number of cases is generally a leading indicator of
subsequent increases in the hospitalization rate. The Health Department had indicated that
unless the hospitalization rate decreased below 10 per 100,000 by Thursday July 28, 2022,
the Health Department would have caused a new mask order to go into effect on Friday July
29, 2022.

Based on telebriefings, other communications, and past health orders from the Health
Department, it was expected that the mask mandate would have applied indoors to anyone
age two or older at facilities such as shared office space, manufacturing and retail settings,
event spaces, restaurants and bars, gyms and yoga studios, educational settings and
children’s programs. Under the health order, businesses would likely have been required
to offer employees masks and notify them of mask-wearing requirements. Additionally,
businesses would be obligated to place signage informing customers of indoor masking.
Such masking order would likely have been in effect until the County experienced at least
two weeks at the “medium” community level.

It is expected that if, in the future, the number of COVID cases in Los Angeles County rose,
that the Health Department may opt to issue County-wide health orders to require masks to
prevent the spread of COVID-19.

This resolution is intended to allow the public to choose for themselves whether to wear a
mask in public. This resolution would result in a commitment to not use city resources to
enforce against the public any future COVID-related indoor mask mandate of the Los
Angeles County Health Department.

FISCAL IMPACT
Possible cost savings by allowing staff and the sheriff to do other work.

  RESOLUTION NO. CC 2022-089

  A RESOLUTION OF THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF PALMDALE
  DIRECTING CITY STAFF AND THE SHERIFF TO NOT ENFORCE
  AGAINST THE PUBLIC COVID-19 RELATED MASK ORDERS OF THE
  LOS ANGELES COUNTY DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH

  WHEREAS, the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health (“Health
Department”), from time-to-time issues orders to the general public, requiring that the
public wear masks in specified locations to deter the spread of COVID-19; and

  WHEREAS, as recently as last week, the Health Department had nearly issued an
order to require indoor use of masks in specified circumstances;

  WHEREAS, the Health Department has its own employees to enforce Health
Department orders; and

  WHEREAS, if Palmdale were to enforce Health Department mask mandates, that
would require the diversion of public resources away from other matters; and

  WHEREAS, the current Los Angeles District Attorney has directed that the District
Attorney’s Department file misdemeanor charges in only very limited circumstances;

  WHEREAS, if the Los Angeles County Sheriff, who provides law enforcement
services in Palmdale, were to arrest any individuals for violations of the County Health
Officer’s orders, it is unlikely that the District Attorney would prosecute any such cases,
and the actions of the Sheriff would have been wasted;

  WHEREAS, on April 1, 2022, the City Council adopted Ordinance 1577, which,
among other things stated, “Business in Palmdale are prohibited from requiring patrons
or customers to provide any documentation certifying COVID-19 vaccination or post-
transmission recovery to gain access to, entry upon, or service from the business.”

  WHEREAS, it is necessary to protect the fundamental rights of people and allow
the free flow of commerce within the City;

  WHEREAS, the City of Palmdale Charter states its purpose is to “restore to our
community the historic principles of self-governance inherent in the doctrine of home-
rule.”

THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF PALMDALE
DOES HEREBY FIND, DETERMINE, RESOLVE AND ORDER AS FOLLOWS:

  Section 1. Non-Enforcement. The City Council hereby declares that the Sheriff
and city staff should not take action to enforce against the public any COVID-related mask
order of the Health Department.
